item.title: Mike LaFleur says he feels "good" about Jeremiyah Love's chances for Week 1
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love injured his ankle in an Aug. 13 preseason game against the Raiders.
item.content:encoded:
Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love injured his ankle in an Aug. 13 preseason game against the Raiders. It was diagnosed as a high-ankle sprain, and he has not practiced or played since.

Love is moving closer to a return, though, and coach Mike LaFleur insinuated that the rookie did something on the practice field Monday.

"Progressing," LaFleur said, via Bo Brack of PHNX Cardinals. "He was out there moving around today. We'll see on Wednesday. I'll have a better idea for all those guys [who are injured]."

The Cardinals will have their first injury report of the season on Wednesday, which will be the first indication of where Love is in his rehab. LaFleur was asked about his optimism for the third overall pick to play against the Chargers.

"Yeah, I feel good," LaFleur said.

Love had 14 touches for 73 yards in the first half of the only preseason game he played.

item.title: Bill Belichick, to no surprise, has little to say about expanding UNC investigation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Despite the team's 1-0 record, a storm has been blowing through the North Carolina football program, with most of it playing out privately.
item.content:encoded:
Despite the team's 1-0 record, a storm has been blowing through the North Carolina football program, with most of it playing out privately.

The situation became much more public last Thursday, with the abrupt resignation of G.M. Mike Lombardi followed by a report from WRAL indicating that the investigation that started with Lombardi has expanded to include defensive coordinator Steve Belichick and others.

Head coach Bill Belichick met with reporters on Monday, for the first time since the situation hit the fan. To no surprise, Belichick didn't have much to say in response to multiple questions about Lombardi, Steve Belichick, and the overall program.

The questions were posed despite an opening comment from a team spokesperson before Belichick took the podium, via WRAL: “Coach Belichick, student athletes, and other university employees will not discuss the situation in any manner. That is necessary to protect the integrity of the process and the rights of everyone involved.”

In his own introductory remarks, Bill Belichick mentioned “the importance of the work that's being done by the investigative team and, obviously, our high standard here of our code of conduct and doing things the right way and making sure that our student-athletes are given the utmost, the best treatment, the very best care, and the very best coaching that we can possibly give them."

He was then peppered with inquiries about the investigation, despite the effort to avoid talking about it.

The mere existence of an investigation that is exploring the behavior of multiple football employees shows that there's at least a question about whether the "high standard here of our code of conduct" has been met — including the question of whether the head coach knew about any of the potential irregularities and failed to report them.

Bill Belichick's potential failure to report issues of which he was aware becomes a potential recipe for a termination "for cause," which would cut off his buyout.

Frankly, the entire situation feels like an effort to find something that would give UNC an escape hatch from a hiring it already regrets, the upset win over TCU notwithstanding. And it creates an overriding vibe that his departure is inevitable. Possibly with no further financial obligation from the school to its second-year head coach.

item.title: Giants cut Darius Slayton
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The veteran wide receiver, who signed a three-year, $36 million contract last season, is out.
item.content:encoded:
Darius Slayton recently said he didn’t pay attention to rumors that he was at risk of getting cut. Apparently he should have.

The Giants announced today that they are releasing Slayton.

The move comes as a surprise if only because of Slayton's contract: Just last year, he signed a three-year, $36 million contract, and he is guaranteed $9.75 million this year. Cutting him only saves the Giants $2.5 million, but apparently they're down enough on him that they thought that savings was worth sending him packing.

The Giants presumably tried to trade Slayton before cutting him and found that no one wanted to trade for that contract.

Slayton caught 37 passes for 538 yards and one touchdown last season, and he's still good enough that some team will surely pick him up. Just not at anything close to what the Giants were paying him.

item.title: Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins return to Bengals practice
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Bengals didn't show concern about wide receivers Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins missing Week 1 when they missed practice last week and the outlook continues to be good as they move closer to Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
The Bengals didn't show concern about wide receivers Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins missing Week 1 when they missed practice last week and the outlook continues to be good as they move closer to Week 1.

Chase and Higgins returned to practice on Monday. Chase hyperextended his knee in a practice and Higgins has been dealing with a heel contusion. Defensive end Shemar Stewart also practiced after returning to the field from a knee injury last week and head coach Zac Taylor made it sound like all three are on track to play.

"All three looked good today," Taylor said at his press conference. "We'll wait to release injury reports on Wednesday, but I was encouraged by the progress all three of those guys have made."

The Bengals would like to get off to a fast start this season and having all three players on the field against the Bucs would be a good step in that direction.

item.title: Newcomer Zaire Franklin named a Packers captain, along with four repeat captains from 2025
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: It didn't take long for new Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin to establish himself as a team leader.
item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for new Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin to establish himself as a team leader.

Franklin, who arrived in Green Bay via a trade in March, has been named one of the Packers' captains. That's not a surprise, as Franklin was a team captain on the Colts in each of the last six seasons. Some players exude leadership, and Franklin is one of them.

The Packers named five captains, Franklin and four players who were also Packers captains last year: quarterback Jordan Love, tight end Tucker Kraft, safety Xavier McKinney and special teamer Isaiah McDuffie.

Three players who were Packers team captains last year are not captains this year: Rashan Gary and Quay Walker, who are no longer in Green Bay, and Josh Jacobs, who is currently on the commissioner's exempt list amid an investigation into an accusation of violence against a woman.

item.content:encoded:
The Patriots listed three players as out of practice on Sunday and they got one of them back on the field Monday.

Defensive tackle Christian Barmore was listed as a full participant. He did not practice on Sunday because of a knee injury and his return to the field bodes well for his chances of playing against the Seahawks on Wednesday night.

Running back TreVeyon Henderson's chances of playing don't look as good. Henderson missed another practice with his ankle injury and has not been on the field in a couple of weeks.

Offensive lineman Ben Brown was the third player out on Sunday and the Patriots announced he will miss the game with a knee injury.

item.title: Mike McCarthy hopeful that Joey Porter will play Week 1
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Steelers do not negotiate contract extensions once the season starts.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers do not negotiate contract extensions once the season starts. Thus, time is running out for the team to complete a long-term deal with cornerback Joey Porter.

"It’s a business, and there's definitely business conversations going on," head coach McCarthy said Monday, via Jack Markowski of SI.com.

McCarthy insinuated that he expects Porter to play regardless how talks turn out before Sunday's season opener against the Falcons.

"Yeah, I hope so," McCarthy said. "You know, just keep working him. He's still, I'd put him in a ramp-up mode."

When asked what happens if Porter doesn't play, McCarthy said, “We’ll see what happens.”

Porter practiced for the first time last Tuesday after spending all of training camp on the active/physically unable to perform list. But last week he was noncommittal about playing Week 1 absent a contract extension.

Porter, a second-round pick in 2023, is entering the final year of his rookie contract scheduled to make $3.924 million this year.

He is coming off a career year, totaling a career-high 14 passes defensed to go along with 52 tackles, one sack and one interception.

item.title: Lions sign LB Joe Bachie to active roster
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Lions have filled one of the openings on their active roster.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions have filled one of the openings on their active roster.

They announced that they have signed linebacker Joe Bachie off of their practice squad. Bachie spent the offseason and preseason with the team and signed to the practice squad after failing to make the initial 53-man roster in Detroit.

Bachie opened last season with the Colts and started five games before landing on injured reserve. He moved on to the Titans after being released and played in 10 more games on special teams. He finished the year with 29 tackles and had 48 tackles in 51 games for the Bengals and Eagles earlier in his career.

The Lions still have one open spot on the 53-man roster after waiving center Seth McLaughlin and running back Jabari Small last week. They announced that both those players have been signed to the practice squad on Monday.

item.title: Bryce Underwood is Michigan's QB "right now," but his job security isn't "infinite"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood saved the Wolverines' bacon with a Hail Mary mulligan.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood saved the Wolverines' bacon with a Hail Mary mulligan. Underwood eventually may not be able to save his starting job.

“He’s our QB right now,” Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham told reporters on Monday, via Nick Kosko of On3.com. “And it’s not something that’s infinite. At some point, we’ve got to turn a corner and we’ve got to see improvement, as we do with a lot of stuff; you’ve got to see improvement out of the coaches, so it’s not just on Bryce. And it’s not just Bryce’s job that is not absolutely set in concrete. You’ve got to perform week in and week out and become somebody that is playing at a level we can win with.”

The program has made a significant financial commitment to Underwood, at $3 million per year. It's one of the realities of paying players; you need to pay the right ones.

Again, Underwood still has the job. Saturday night's performance against a MAC school was troubling, even with the late-game heroics. Underwood completed 12 of 22 passes for 170 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. He added 47 yards rushing and a touchdown, on nine attempts.

He'll need to perform at a higher level against better competition.

The next test happens on Saturday, when Oklahoma comes to town.

item.title: Steelers won't have full-season captains under Mike McCarthy
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: It's currently team captain season, with plenty of NFL franchises unveiling plenty of season-long captains.
item.content:encoded:
It's currently team captain season, with plenty of NFL franchises unveiling plenty of season-long captains. In Pittsburgh, however, there won't be a tweet with anywhere from five to 11 players listed as those who will be wearing a "C" in 2026.

New coach Mike McCarthy told reporters on Monday that he won’t use full-season captains. Instead, he'll name captains for each week’s game. That's how McCarthy handled the captain designations while serving as the head coach of the Packers and the Cowboys.

The approach is a clear departure from past practices under Mike Tomlin, and another clear sign that some things will be very different with one Mike yielding to another.

Last year, the Steelers had four permanent captains: quarterback Aaron Rodgers, defensive lineman Cameron Heyward, linebacker T.J. Watt, and safety Miles Killebrew. (After Killebrew was lost for the season due to injury, linebacker Payton Wilson replaced Killebrew as the special-teams captain.)

item.title: Alec Pierce is expected to play for the Colts in Week 1
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce has been back at practice for a little over a week, but that's been enough time for the team to see what they needed from the wideout.
item.content:encoded:
Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce has been back at practice for a little over a week, but that's been enough time for the team to see what they needed from the wideout.

Pierce had ankle surgery this offseason and set playing in Week 1 as his goal throughout his recovery process. The finish line is days away and it appears Pierce is going to make it.

At a Monday press conference, head coach Shane Steichen said, via multiple reporters, that Pierce "should be good to go" against the Ravens.

Keenan Allen is also expected to play after being arrested in the hours after the team's final preseason game and tight end Tyler Warren has returned from a groin injury, so the Colts are set to have their full receiving corps available for Daniel Jones's first game since tearing his Achilles last season.

item.title: Cowboys LG Tyler Smith to have thumb surgery, miss 4-6 weeks
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Cowboys are going to be missing a starting offensive lineman for the first chunk of the regular season.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys are going to be missing a starting offensive lineman for the first chunk of the regular season.

Head coach Brian Schottenheimer told reporters at a Monday press conference that left guard Tyler Smith is going to have thumb surgery. Smith is expected to miss 4-6 weeks as a result of the operation.

Smith is set to go on injured reserve, so the Cowboys will be able to replace him on the active roster. They open the season against the Giants on Sunday night and then face the Commanders, Ravens, Texans, Buccaneers, and Packers in the first six weeks of the season.

TJ Bass is set to fill in at left guard until Smith is able to return to action.

item.title: Tua Tagovailoa's return to Pittsburgh puts extra pressure on Mike McCarthy's debut
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The last time quarterback Tua Tagovailoa started a game in Pittsburgh, it became his last start with the Miami Dolphins.
item.content:encoded:
The last time quarterback Tua Tagovailoa started a game in Pittsburgh, it became his last start with the Miami Dolphins. He was benched after the 28-15 loss on a Monday night in December — and he was cut in March.

Fast forward to September, and Tua will be returning to Pittsburgh as the Week 1 starter for the Falcons.

If it goes poorly, Tua may not be starting for very long. If it goes well, and if the Falcons upset the Steelers (Pittsburgh is currently favored by 3.5 points), there will be a very strong reaction in Western Pennsylvania.

Losing to Tua after drubbing him less than nine months earlier will provide the first clear apples-to-apples comparison between new coach Mike McCarthy and his predecessor, Mike Tomlin. Nuances will easily be lost on Steelers Nation. Yes, the Falcons are an overall better team than the 2025 Dolphins. The common denominator is the quarterback; if he plays dramatically better than he did the last time he played in Pittsburgh, Steelers fans will interpret that as an indication that the new boss won't have the same kind of success as the old boss.

It would be dubbed an overreaction. But that's what football fans do. With only seventeen games in a season, they all count. They all spark a reaction. And, at some point, the trend of overreacting shows that, actually, it's the normal and usual reaction to a team losing a game it should have won.

The Steelers have more than a few winnable games in the eight weeks before the bye, including two against the Browns. Anything less than 5-3 will spark high anxiety on and after Week 10, where the Eagles, Broncos, Texans, Jaguars, a road game at the Bengals, and two games against the Ravens are lurking.

The fans who show up in six days will be expecting a 1-0 start. If the end result is 0-1, sphincters will be tightening quickly in the Steel City.

item.title: Past proposals to show tenths of a second on NFL stadium clocks have gone nowhere
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the football-following world continues to process the implausible outcome of Saturday night's Western Michigan-Michigan game, it makes sense to consider any and all ideas for avoiding a similar outcome — at the college level or in the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
As the football-following world continues to process the implausible outcome of Saturday night's Western Michigan-Michigan game, it makes sense to consider any and all ideas for avoiding a similar outcome — at the college level or in the NFL.

Current NFL rules would have not given Michigan a mulligan, because matters of clock timing can't be reviewed unless two or more seconds remain.

Another NFL rule would have slammed the door on an extra snap for the Wolverines; as former NFL senior V.P. of officiating Mike Pereira told The Athletic, the pro football protocol entails relying on the stadium clock that is visible to everyone — not a separate clock seen during the replay-review process.

“It is my understanding that if there is a discrepancy between the video and replay command center versus the television network video that everybody sees, that replay is to use the TV video,” Pereira told The Athletic. “And that is the same protocol in the NFL, in the UFL. It’s the same. You use the footage that everybody sees if there is a discrepancy.”

There's another potential safeguard that could be employed in such situations, at both levels: clocks showing tenths of a second, when the time slips under one minute.

The Eagles proposed this approach twice in recent years, in 2023 and most recently in 2024. The effort failed in 2023 because many of the existing clocks weren’t capable of showing tenths of seconds, and teams didn’t want to spend the money to adapt to the new rule. The proposal failed in 2024, too.

Pennywise. Pound foolish. If/when the NFL experiences a scandal similar to the one that played out in Ann Arbor, the owners will wish they'd written the checks for new clocks.

item.title: Former Bears FB Matt Suhey dies at 68
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Matt Suhey, a member of the Bears' Super Bowl XX champions, has died.
item.content:encoded:
Matt Suhey, a member of the Bears' Super Bowl XX champions, has died.

The Bears confirmed to the Associated Press that Suhey died at the age of 68. No cause of death was given.

Suhey was a 1980 second-round pick after playing at Penn State and spent most of his 10 seasons with the Bears as a lead blocker for Walter Payton. That run included the franchise's only Super Bowl win and Suhey ran for his only career postseason touchdown in Chicago's rout of the Patriots that secured the Lombardi Trophy.

Suhey, who spent his entire career with the Bears, ran 898 times for 2,946 yards and 20 touchdowns in 148 regular season games. He also caught 260 passes for 2,113 yards and five touchdowns over his decade in the NFL.

item.title: Michael Penix: I'm close to 100 percent, but I'm not there yet
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski named Tua Tagovailoa the team's starting quarterback for the first game of the season on Monday and that decision was not made over any objection from Michael Penix.
item.content:encoded:
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski named Tua Tagovailoa the team's starting quarterback for the first game of the season on Monday and that decision was not made over any objection from Michael Penix.

Penix was cleared for 11-on-11 work near the end of August and the quarterback said on Monday that he told Stefanski that he still does not feel like he's fully recovered from last year's torn ACL. Penix, who will be inactive in Week 1, said that he wants "to be stronger" and that it isn't fair to the team to try to go out there until "there's no doubt in my mind that I trust my knee."

"I just told him I'm not where I want to be right now," Penix said, via the team's website. "And I want to be able to be 100 percent so I can help the team win football games. And I'm really close. Really close."

Penix has recovered from two other torn ACLs and said that he feels like he tried to come back too soon in the past, so he wants to avoid a similar situation this time. That opens the door for Tagovailoa to seize the job more convincingly than he did this summer, but that's a risk that Penix appears to be more comfortable with than any having to do with his health.

item.title: Todd Monken: There could be a package of plays for QB Taylen Green
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Deshaun Watson will be starting at quarterback for the Browns in Week 1, but head coach Todd Monken left the door open to the possibility that another quarterback could also see playing time against the Jaguars.
item.content:encoded:
Deshaun Watson will be starting at quarterback for the Browns in Week 1, but head coach Todd Monken left the door open to the possibility that another quarterback could also see playing time against the Jaguars.

Rookie Taylen Green made the 53-man roster and Monken was asked at a Monday press conference if the team could possibly have a package of plays in the playbook to take advantage of the sixth-round pick's athleticism.

"There could be a package where we have him," Monken said.

Monken went on to stress that it is a possibility rather than something the team is actively planning to have in place and that "three's a lot" when asked about having Green active alongside Watson and backup Shedeur Sanders. The Jaguars probably won't be losing much sleep about that possibility, but it will be something to watch out for if Green avoids the inactive list on Sunday afternoon.

item.title: Lane Kiffin on his haltfime wisecrack: "Everybody hates you. They can't hate you much more."
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: At halftime of Saturday night's 51-10 blowout win over Clemson, when LSU won 31-3, Tigers coach Lane Kiffin capped an on-field interview by saying, "Imagine if we had pro players."
item.content:encoded:
At halftime of Saturday night's 51-10 blowout win over Clemson, when LSU won 31-3, Tigers coach Lane Kiffin capped an on-field interview by saying, "Imagine if we had pro players."

After the game, Kiffin was asked about his halftime wisecrack.

"What's the difference?" Kiffin said. "Everybody hates you. They can't hate you that much more. So there you go. You got another line."

Kiffin took comfort in the fact that the NFL transfer storyline didn't loom over the outcome of the game.

"I'm just really glad they played the way they did, so that wouldn't have been the story," Kiffin said. "Because I get it . . . even if we won close and kind of ugly, the whole story would have been, 'Man, I screwed the team up by doing this.' And I said this morning, 'You can not agree with it. I've been criticized heavily for the last two weeks saying I did that.' . . . But my job is not to please you and worry about what you're going to write. My job is what I believe is right, and I believe we're fighting for what was right for those kids.

"I'm not going to get into all the reasons, but that's what I believe. And so many people don't like that, but they don't understand that."

Still, Kiffin knew or should have known that his effort to bring back players with NFL offseason and preseason experience would have sparked a backlash, especially at a time when the powers-that-be are looking for anything they can use to get Congress to clean up the mess that has flowed directly from the implosion of decades of antitrust violations.

They've been huffing and puffing about "pro players" returning to college football, while ignoring the fact that college football players have become pro players. They've been glossing over the fact that Nick Saban once brought an NFL free agent (Trent Richardson) back to campus to practice against college players. And they've been sinking their teeth into the disingenuous notion that the returning pro players will displace current players, ignoring the basic reality that current players get displaced all the time, by transfers and other incoming recruits.

Yes, he may be naturally inclined to wear a black hat. Or maybe he's just not afraid to do what's right for his team, even if the strategy plays directly into the hands of those who hope to parlay the current chaos into an antitrust exemption that allows player income to be restricted and player mobility to be limited.

item.title: LSU fans had a strong reaction to an image of Jayden Daniels on the video board
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Three years after quarterback Jayden Daniels put together a Heisman-winning season at LSU, the attitude of the fan base has taken a sharp turn.
item.content:encoded:
Three years after quarterback Jayden Daniels put together a Heisman-winning season at LSU, the attitude of the fan base has taken a sharp turn.

It's a direct result of the recent dust-up over the re-issuance of No. 5, a move to which Daniels had a strong reaction. Beyond launching a thousand jokes, it prompted many of the 100,000-plus who attended Saturday night's Clemson-LSU game to have a strong reaction to an image of Daniels on the video board.

The ESPN college football account on Twitter has posted a clip of former LSU players in the NFL (not to be confused with former NFL players at LSU), cycling through one NFL team at a time.

When the Commanders page landed, showing Daniels and K'Lavon Chaisson, the reaction went from generally positive to loudly negative.

It's no surprise, but it's the first tangible piece of evidence regarding the collective fan reaction to seeing Daniels's name and likeness.

item.title: Lane Kiffin at halftime of 31-3 blowout: "Imagine if we had pro players"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Some regard LSU coach Lane Kiffin as an agent of chaos.
item.content:encoded:
Some regard LSU coach Lane Kiffin as an agent of chaos. The better explanation is that he's a garden-variety troll.

At halftime of Saturday night's weather-delayed game against Clemson, Kiffin was interviewed by ESPN's Holly Rowe. After the interview ended, Kiffin started to walk away before circling back to the microphone and saying, "Imagine if we had pro players."

It was a hilarious reference to the elephant that has resided in the room for the past several weeks. Kiffin has been trying to add players who should have been eligible for another season, and who pursued NFL careers until their right to one more college season was recognized by the courts. It has sparked outcries from many that "professional" players should be excluded from college football — which ignores the reality that college players are now professional players.

Without the two players that LSU decided not to add to the roster for the opening game, given the possibility that the SEC could retaliate by kicking them out of the conference, Kiffin and company are still manhandling Clemson.

item.title: Mike Vrabel wants to be involved in resolving Christian Gonzalez situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: In three days, the Patriots face the Seahawks in a rematch of Super Bowl LX.
item.content:encoded:
In three days, the Patriots face the Seahawks in a rematch of Super Bowl LX. It remains to be seen whether cornerback Christian Gonzalez will have a new contract and, if not, whether he'll play.

Gonzalez hasn’t committed to playing without his new deal, which means there's a non-zero-percent chance he won't.

On Saturday, coach Mike Vrabel was asked whether he will share his "two cents" or "go to bat" for Gonzalez.

"I think it's an interesting dynamic," Vrabel told reporters. "I’ve been on both sides. I think what's important for me is to try to communicate, try to explain [to] the players that we really want to build around and have. I’ve done that with Gonzo, and everybody knows that. So, I don’t get involved in the negotiations per se, but I certainly want to be involved in trying to get the situation resolved. That's really what I try to do throughout my job, my day here, is what the issues are, what's in front of us and what we have to do to help the team. It's a delicate balance. . . . I want to be able to just continue to prepare for Seattle and focus on all the things that we’re going to have to do to beat an excellent football team with our team and the players that we have and how we get off to a really good start here."

Gonzalez has called the situation frustrating. Vrabel was asked whether he shares that feeling.

"I wouldn’t use the word frustrating," Vrabel said. "Again, I appreciate how our players feel and their emotions, and I think that's part of life. But I can’t let that be frustrating. I want to be able to coach him, help him improve as a player and a person, help our football team and help our coaches."

Vrabel otherwise provided no firm update on where the situation stands.

"I think whenever the deal is done, that's when it’ll be resolved," Vrabel said. "I don’t know. I don’t have a timetable. I’ve tried to do a good job of communicating with everybody involved the best that I can."

Does he have confidence a deal will get done?

"I would say when it gets done, that's really what the confidence level is," Vrabel said. "There's no, ‘Is it almost done? Is it not almost done?’ I don’t want to deal with hypotheticals or speculation. It's important to focus on Seattle. And again, I do appreciate and understand what you guys feel like is important. I just know what's important for us is how we prepare. This is a good football team. This is an excellent football team. I told our team if we don’t play better than we played the last time we played them, we’re going to struggle."

They'll struggle more without Gonzalez to assist in covering players like Jaxon Smith-Njiba and Rashid Shaheed. And Vrabel's plan for the game will need to take into account the possibility that he won't have Gonzalez.

The Patriots went through this before, in 2020. Not long before Week 1, cornerback Stephon Gilmore made it clear that he wouldn't be playing without an adjustment to his contract. In that case, it was fairly simple; the Patriots moved $5 million in 2021 compensation to 2020. This time, it will require a commitment that exceeds the deal done by Seahawks cornerback Devon Witherspoon at $33 million per year in new money, 22 days ago.

Whatever the snags (we're told it's a combination of dollars and structure, which doesn't narrow it down by much), there's an obvious sticking point that has yet to become unstuck. And it sets the stage for Gonzalez declining to play without an agreement — which could, depending on how the team reacts to a player who is under contract and with the team refusing to work, make things very interesting.

It's essentially a one-man wildcat strike. And the team would have rights under the Collective Bargaining Agreement. Exercising those rights, however, wouldn't do much to enhance the long-term relationship between the team and one of its most important players.

item.title: Under NFL rules, Michigan wouldn't have gotten a final play
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Current college rules set the stage for a controversial one-second hair-splitting.
item.content:encoded:
Various differences exist between the NFL rulebook and the college football rules. One specific variation would have prevented the controversial outcome to Saturday night's game between Western Michigan and Michigan.

The game-winning Hail Mary touchdown reception by J.J. Buchanan never would have happened under NFL rules, because NFL rules account for the possibility of a razor-thin margin between the clock being at one second and the clock showing triple zeroes.

From Rule 15, Article 9(b) of the official 2026 NFL rulebook: "An on-field ruling that time expired during or after the last play of any half, or of an overtime period in the regular season, or of an overtime half in the postseason, is reviewable by the Replay Official only when the visual evidence demonstrates that the clock should have stopped with two or more seconds remaining." (Emphasis added.)

The Michigan controversy comes down to whether the clock showed one second or no time remaining when a Western Michigan player touched a Hail Mary attempt that sailed out of the back of the end zone. The Big Ten split hairs in a way that gave Michigan a mulligan.

If this ever happens in the NFL, replay can't change the ruling on the field unless the clock shows at least two or more seconds.

While that doesn't change the fact that the NFL should embrace real-time transparency regarding the replay process, this is one very specific situation that would have made the final outcome far simpler. With no question that fewer than two seconds remained, the offense would not have gotten another attempt, because the rules would not have allowed the ruling on the field to be changed.

Moving forward, adopting that rule would be the best way for college football to avoid a repeat of what happened last night. Even if it may not happen again for a very long time.

item.title: NFL announces new contract for Roger Goodell
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Goodell is now signed through March 31, 2031.
item.content:encoded:
Little more than 20 years after he signed his first contract to be the Commissioner of the National Football League, Roger Goodell has put his name at the bottom of the newest one.

The NFL announced on Sunday afternoon that the league's Compensation Committee has informed the full membership that an agreement has been reached on a four-year extension. Goodell is now under contract through March 31, 2031.

His prior deal would have expired in March 2027. With few if any obvious successors in play, Goodell had plenty of leverage.

In the memo to all owners, a copy of which PFT has obtained, Patriots owner Robert Kraft explained that the Committee "worked closely with an independent third-party compensation consultant and outside counsel to structure a deal that aligns Roger’s compensation with the League’s long-term interests and success."

The contract ties 95 percent of the total compensation to Goodell's and the league's "performance measured against various metrics and at the discretion of the Compensation Committee."

When the league office was structured as a tax-exempt trade association, the NFL was required to disclose Goodell's compensation on an annual basis. Since the league pivoted away from that approach, there has been no true clarity as to his total pay.

It is surely substantial, most likely more than any player earns. And it's not hard to argue that Goodell has earned his keep, given the manner in which the sport has continued to grow, with ever-increasing profits and staggering franchise values.

He also continues to provide a valuable service to his 32 bosses, taking the public heat for any and all potentially unpopular policies or decisions.

Goodell's extension covers the duration of the current broadcast deals, which means that he'll be in the captain's chair for the next wave of TV and streaming contracts. The deal ends, however, not long after the expiration of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement with the NFL Players Association.

Absent an early renegotiation with the NFLPA, the league will need another new deal with Goodell (who will be 72 at the time) or an effective transition plan to be implemented during a potential lockout aimed at securing an 18-game regular season and 16 annual international games.

The news comes three days before the start of Goodell's 21st season at the helm of the sport, at the otherwise quiet midpoint of Labor Day weekend.

item.title: Arizona State, Morgan State agreed to reduce fourth quarter of blowout to 10 minutes
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On the same day that a college football game consisted of one second more than 60 minutes, another college football game had five minutes fewer than the usual amount.
item.content:encoded:
On the same day that a college football game consisted of one second more than 60 minutes, another college football game had five minutes fewer than the usual amount.

Like many early-season games featuring an established program against an FCS slappie, Saturday's game between Arizona State and Morgan State turned into a blowout. Andwith the Sun Devils leading 70-7 after three quarters, the two teams agreed to shrink the fourth quarter to 10 minutes.

“I’ve never been a part of a game like that," Arizona State coach Kenny Dilligham told reporters after the game, via Bailey Leasure of ArizonaSports.com. "I didn’t even know that was legal, but I learned something today. When he asked to shorten it. I said, ‘Whatever he wants, we’ll do.'"

Arizona State had scored 28 points, 21 points, and 21 points in the first three quarters, respectively. Neither team scored in the final 10 minutes, which consisted of 19 total plays.

It's a strange outcome, to say the least. And it opens the door to a situation in which certain potential wagers would be undermined by a 60-minute game shrinking unexpectedly to 55 minutes.

But it also opens the door to a new universe of potential prediction markets: Will the game be shortened by the agreement of the teams for reasons other than the weather?

item.title: All 2026 quarterback competitions went to the older players
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Training camp opened with four, and potentially five, NFL quarterback competitions.
item.content:encoded:
Training camp opened with four, and potentially five, NFL quarterback competitions.

In the end, all five jobs went to the older of the two primary contenders.

The first decision came in Minnesota, where Kyler Murray prevailed over 2024 top-10 selection J.J. McCarthy in the first competition to be resolved, before the first preseason game. The backup job there also has apparently gone to the older player, with Carson Wentz seemingly leapfrogging McCarthy. (The Vikings have yet to release their Week 1 depth chart.)

Minnesota will enter the season with three former high first-round picks in their quarterback room. Murray was No. 1 overall in 2019, and Wentz was the second overall pick in 2016.

The next decision was made by the Browns, where Deshaun Watson was made the starter (at least for Week 1 and likely Week 2) two weeks ago today, over 2025 fifth-rounder Shedeur Sanders. Watson was the 12th overall pick in 2017.

Last week, the Raiders finally declared that Kirk Cousins, who entered the league as a fourth-round pick in 2012, would start Week 1 over Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick in 2026.

And now the Falcons have gone with Tua Tagovailoa, pick No. 5 in 2020, over Michael Penix Jr., the eighth overall selection in 2024. That one feels even more tenuous than Watson in Cleveland; the Falcons were hoping Penix would be ready to go. Ultimately, they decided he wasn't — and Tua got the nod over Cooper Rush (who's technically older than Tua).

The fifth competition never became one, because Jacoby Brissett got a new deal done before a hold in gave Gardner Minshew or Carson Beck a chance to learn the new offense and potentially supplant Brissett.

In many situations, winning the starting job to start the season means securing the privilege of eventually being benched. That's a very real possibility for Watson, Cousins, and Tagovailoa. The safest of them all is Murray, who was likely signed to be the starter — and who is playing for a team that wants to have the same quarterback in place for all 17 regular-season games.

item.title: Western Michigan-Michigan outcome created chaos for Kalshi
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Last night's chaotic outcome to the Western Michigan-Michigan game created true chaos for the prediction markets, which have learned a valuable lesson once taught by Yogi Berra.
item.content:encoded:
Last night's chaotic outcome to the Western Michigan-Michigan game created true chaos for the prediction markets, which have learned a valuable lesson once taught by Yogi Berra.

It ain't over 'til it's over.

Via Marshall Cohen of CNN, Kalshi confirmed that it prematurely, and incorrectly, treated the game as a Western Michigan win. Kalshi later flipped the outcome, taking back money from the winners, reimbursing the losers, and then making the accurate payouts.

In all, Kalshi had $18.6 million in volume on the game.

Hopefully, Kalshi and Polymarket will be a little more patient the next time something like this happens. Otherwise, it'll be déjà vu all over again.

item.title: Todd Monken names Deshaun Watson one of five Week 1 captains
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: For at least one week, Deshaun Watson will be a Browns captain.
item.content:encoded:
For at least one week, Deshaun Watson will be a Browns captain.

Head coach Todd Monken named Watson one of Cleveland’s five captains for the season opener against Jacksonville. Monken explained that the team will not have season-long captains, instead doing them weekly. There will be two captains from offense, two from defense, and one from special teams chosen by the coaches.

And in Week 1, Watson — the starting quarterback — will be one of the offensive representatives.

“It’ll vary week-to-week, and then at the end of the year, the players will vote on the permanent 2026 captains,” Monken said in his Monday press conference. “I just like it that way. I think we have a fairly young team. I’m not ready to name guys that are permanent for us. I do think it’s cool for players to go out for the coin toss, I think it’s really cool.

“I think most teams have more leaders than just four or five guys — I just believe that. I believe that with each game you reward guys for the week that they’ve had, and that’s what we’re going to do.”

Watson, guard Zion Johnson, cornerback Tyson Campbell, defensive tackle Mason Graham, and long snapper Rex Sunahara will be the Browns’ Week 1 captains.

Kickoff between the Browns and Jaguars is set for 1 p.m. ET in Jacksonville on Sunday.

item.title: Dan Campbell says Lions' backup running backs will be a two-man committee
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Lions have the highest-paid running back in the NFL, Jahmyr Gibbs, as their starter.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions have the highest-paid running back in the NFL, Jahmyr Gibbs, as their starter. Behind him, they have two other running backs on the roster: Sione Vaki, who has seven carries for 18 yards in his NFL career, and Jacob Saylors, who has two carries for 11 yards in his NFL career. That makes depth at running back a major concern.

Or at least it would seem to be, but Lions head coach Dan Campbell said the Lions will be fine playing running-back-by-committee with Saylors and Vaki if needed.

"It's by committee," Campbell said. "I see Vaki getting some reps too. I don't see it like Saylors is running back 2. Saylors brings special teams value and there's things he's been able to do. We've seen more of him than Vaki in games, preseason games, but Vaki had some pretty good reps in practice, and we know Vaki is a very valuable special teams player, too. But we feel like Vaki is ready to take some of this on as a runner and pass protector and receiver. So we feel good with either one of those guys in there when Jah needs a breather."

After trading David Montgomery to Houston, the Lions expect to give Gibbs a bigger workload than he's ever had before. But Gibbs won't be on the field for every play, and Vaki and Saylors also will get a heavier workload.
